summary: Ember Atlas puts every NASA microgravity combustion test we could find into one cited, searchable atlas for crew-habitat fire safety. Using NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) API, we imported 2,008 test records from 21 investigations, checksummed each table, converted units in code and flagged 28 data-entry problems openly. The atlas answers the challenge's Moon base question directly: NASA burned fuel droplets at exactly 30% oxygen and 71 kPa (eight FLEX tests); the closest solid-material fire is Saffire VI-3; and drop-tower tests show three materials burning at lower oxygen at lunar gravity than in orbit or on Earth. An oxygen pressure map, a nearest-test engine, an animated 3D lab and an AI research companion powered by Anthropic's Claude, citing NASA findings and test rows, make that evidence easy to use and check.
details:
What it does and how it works

Ember Atlas answers a question NASA’s archive could not answer in a click: has NASA ever burned anything at a Moon base atmosphere (30% oxygen at 10.2 psi)? It combines 2,008 test records from 21 NASA combustion investigations in one searchable atlas.

  • Atlas map: 754 tests plotted by oxygen and pressure, with crew atmospheres marked. Click any point for its tests and NASA record.
  • Nearest-test engine: set any cabin atmosphere and see the closest real NASA tests, condition by condition: what matches, what differs, and what NASA never recorded.
  • AI research companion: Anthropic’s Claude answers questions from NASA’s actual test rows and cites each one. Ask which BASS-II run spread fastest and it answers “M16, 0.144 mm/s at 5 cm/s”. It declines to invent numbers.
  • Mission desk: ranks investigations for any habitat and safety question, with a stated reason for each rank.
  • 3D combustion lab: an animated flame illustrating gravity, oxygen, airflow and pressure.

The Moon base is our headline example, not the limit. The same search works for any cabin: set oxygen (15–40%), pressure (50–110 kPa), airflow, fuel and gravity (orbit, Moon, Mars, Earth) and Ember Atlas finds the nearest real NASA tests. It covers orbital habitats, lunar bases, Mars habitats and pressurized rovers, and charts NASA’s measured flammability limits at both lunar and Martian gravity

What we found with it:

  • Liquid fuel: yes. Eight FLEX tests burned droplets at exactly 30% oxygen and 71–72 kPa on the ISS.
  • Solid materials: not yet. The closest is Saffire VI-3, at lower pressure. That is the missing experiment.
  • Lunar gravity may be worse than both orbit and Earth. In NASA drop-tower tests, Mylar burned down to 15.6% oxygen at lunar gravity, against 17.0% in microgravity and 21.2% on Earth.

Benefits

  • Finding the nearest NASA fire test to a cabin design takes seconds, with the source table attached, where it took us days.
  • Every number is traceable: each file is checksummed and each record keeps NASA’s original cell.
  • We found and openly list 28 errors in NASA’s published tables (for example, 34% oxygen written as “3400%”), so users know which values to trust.
  • Any dataset downloads as CSV; any scenario exports as a one-page brief or a shareable link.

Intended impact

To help habitat designers, researchers and students make fire-safety decisions for the Moon and Mars from real evidence, and to show where that evidence runs out. Our clearest result is a concrete next step for NASA: test a solid material at the Moon base atmosphere. The data also suggests Earth-based flammability screening may not be conservative at lunar gravity.

Tools, languages and software

TypeScript, Next.js 16 and React 19; Three.js for the 3D flame; SVG for charts; Zod for validation; Node.js scripts for data import. Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 through the Vercel AI SDK and AI Gateway. Hosted on Vercel at emberatlas.tech with no database or login. Data comes from NASA’s PSI public API and NASA technical reports (NTRS). 36 automated tests. Development was assisted by Claude Code.

How it is creative

  • We treated the challenge as a detective question, not a dashboard: one sharp question, answered three ways.
  • The AI answers from the data itself. The server picks the exact NASA test rows, and any answer citing something it was not given is rejected.
  • We turned data-quality problems into a feature: errors are flagged in the open, never silently fixed.
  • The atlas map shows every test against real crew atmospheres, so gaps in NASA’s testing are visible at a glance.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy first: values checked against NASA’s original PDFs; our hand-typed BASS-II numbers match NASA’s table on every run.
  • Honesty about limits: every PSI test ran in microgravity; the lunar-gravity results come from 5-second tests on three materials; the 3D flame is an illustration, not a simulation.
  • Reproducibility: one script re-downloads all 21 tables and verifies them.
  • Accessibility: readable on phones, keyboard-navigable, text alternatives for charts.
  • Cost and reliability: AI answers are cached and rate-limited, with a search-only fallback if the AI is unavailable.
  • Safety: a research and teaching tool, not a certification. AI answers passed 20 of 22 live checks and have not been reviewed by a combustion scientist.
